ad1.html:
Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is Microsoft’s directory service: one central database of identities and resources (users, computers, groups, printers) plus the services that authenticate (prove who you are) and authorize (decide what you can touch). Instead of an account on every PC, you have one account that works across the whole company.

  • Domain controller (DC) — a Windows Server running AD DS. It holds a writable copy of the directory and answers logons. Every serious domain has at least two.
  • Domain — an administrative and replication boundary, named with DNS: corp.local (production uses a real registered name such as ad.example.com).
  • Tree — domains sharing a contiguous DNS namespace (corp.local + sales.corp.local). Forest — one or more trees sharing a schema and Global Catalog. The forest is the real security boundary.
  • NTDS.dit — the database file (C:\Windows\NTDS) on every DC. It contains every account’s password hash, which is why a stolen copy is catastrophic. SYSVOL is the shared folder that holds Group Policy files and logon scripts.

Clients find domain controllers by asking DNS for SRV records such as _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.local. That is why the #1 cause of “the domain is broken” is DNS: a domain-joined PC must use the DC (or an internal DNS server that can resolve the domain) as its DNS server — never a public resolver like 8.8.8.8 as its only DNS.

nslookup -type=SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.local
nltest /dsgetdc:corp.local     # which DC am I talking to?

ad1.h: Objects and how they are named
ad1.html:
Everything in the directory is an object with attributes; the schema defines which object classes and attributes exist. Each object has several names:

NameExampleNotes
sAMAccountNameCORP\jsmithLegacy logon name, 20 characters max, unique in the domain
UPNjsmith@corp.localModern logon name (looks like email)
Distinguished Name (DN)CN=Jane Smith,OU=Sales,DC=corp,DC=localFull path in the tree. CN=common name, OU=organizational unit, DC=domain component. Reads leaf → root.
SIDS-1-5-21-…-1104Security identifier used in permissions. Domain SID + a RID (the last number). Never reused.
GUID128-bit IDNever changes for the life of the object, even if renamed or moved

Permissions are granted to SIDs, not names. Delete and re-create an account with the same name and it is a different SID — it will not have the old account’s access.

PortService
53 TCP/UDPDNS
88 TCP/UDPKerberos authentication
123 UDPTime (NTP / W32Time) — Kerberos needs clocks within 5 minutes
135 TCPRPC endpoint mapper (plus dynamic high ports)
389 TCP/UDPLDAP (directory queries)
636 TCPLDAPS (LDAP over TLS)
445 TCPSMB (file shares, SYSVOL, NETLOGON)
464 TCP/UDPKerberos password change (kpasswd)
3268 / 3269Global Catalog (LDAP / LDAPS)
3389 TCPRDP
9389 TCPActive Directory Web Services (PowerShell AD module)

On-premises AD speaks Kerberos, NTLM, LDAP and applies Group Policy. Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is the cloud identity service: it speaks OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, SAML and the Microsoft Graph API, has no OUs or GPOs, and is not a replacement for domain controllers. Most companies run hybrid: accounts sync from AD to Entra ID with Entra Connect so one identity works on-prem and in Microsoft 365.

ad2.html:
An OU is a folder inside a domain. You create OUs to (1) link Group Policy to a set of objects and (2) delegate administration (for example let the helpdesk reset passwords only in the Sales OU).

  • OU vs group: an OU is a location (an object lives in exactly one OU); a group is a collection (a user can be in many). Group Policy is applied to OUs, not groups (groups can only filter it). Permissions are given to groups, not OUs.
  • The default CN=Users and CN=Computers are containers, not OUs — you cannot link a GPO to them. Create your own OUs and move objects out.
  • Turn on Protect from accidental deletion. New OUs created with PowerShell are protected by default.
  • Design OUs around how you manage things (Workstations, Servers, Staff by department), not around the org chart.

Type: Security groups get permissions and can be used in ACLs. Distribution groups only send email (no permissions).

ScopeMembers can come fromCan be used to grant permissions on
Domain LocalAny domain in the forestResources in its own domain
GlobalIts own domain onlyResources in any domain in the forest
UniversalAny domain in the forestAnywhere (stored in the Global Catalog; changes replicate forest-wide)

Best-practice recipe — AGDLP: Accounts go in Global groups (organized by role: G-Finance); Global groups go in Domain Local groups (organized by resource access: DL-FinanceShare-RW); the Domain Local group gets the Permission on the resource. To give a new hire access, you only add them to one Global group.

• Domain Admins — full control of the domain. Member of every PC’s local Administrators group.
  • Enterprise Admins — full control of the forest; exists only in the forest root domain. Should be empty day-to-day.
  • Schema Admins — can modify the schema. Should be empty except during a change.
  • Administrators (built-in) — local to DCs, includes Domain/Enterprise Admins.
  • Account Operators, Server Operators, Backup Operators, Print Operators — legacy partial-admin groups; Backup Operators can copy NTDS.dit, so treat them as Tier 0. Keep them empty if you can.
  • Domain Users — every user account. Authenticated Users — any identity that logged on (a special identity, not a group you manage).
  • Protected Users — hardening group: no NTLM, no delegation, no cached credentials, short Kerberos TGT lifetimes. Use for admins.

ad2.h: Account states and the user lifecycle
ad2.html:
StateWhat it meansFix
DisabledAn admin turned it offEnable-ADAccount
Locked outToo many bad passwords (policy), clears automatically after the lockout durationUnlock-ADAccount
Account expiredExpiration date passed (contractors)Extend the date
Password expiredOlder than max password ageUser changes it / admin resets it

Joiner → Mover → Leaver (JML): Joiner: create the account in the right OU, add to role groups, set a temporary password with “must change at next logon.” Mover: swap role groups (remove old, add new). Leaver: disable first, move to a Disabled OU, strip privileged groups, note the date in the description, and delete only after the retention period — deleting immediately destroys the SID and any chance to recover files or mailbox.

ad3.html:
The ActiveDirectory PowerShell module (installed with RSAT: Remote Server Administration Tools, or on any DC) talks to AD Web Services (TCP 9389). The GUI equivalents are Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc) and the Active Directory Administrative Center. In real life: Import-Module ActiveDirectory. The lab console already has it loaded.

Get-Command *AD*          # discover cmdlets
Get-Help Get-ADUser -Examples

Get-ADUser jsmith                                   # -Identity (sAMAccountName, DN, SID or GUID)
Get-ADUser -Filter *                                # everyone
Get-ADUser -Filter "Department -eq 'Sales'" -Properties Department
Get-ADUser -Filter "Name -like '*Smith*' -and Enabled -eq $true"
Get-ADUser -Filter * -SearchBase "OU=IT,DC=corp,DC=local"
Get-ADUser jsmith -Properties *                     # every attribute
  • -Identity returns one exact object (errors if missing). -Filter returns zero or more and never errors when nothing matches.
  • By default only ~10 properties come back. Ask for more with -Properties (Department,Title,LastLogonDate,MemberOf) — or * to see everything while exploring.
  • Filter operators are word-style: -eq -ne -like -notlike -gt -lt -and -or -not; -like uses * wildcards. Wrap the filter in quotes.
  • -SearchBase limits the search to an OU (by its DN). -LDAPFilter accepts raw LDAP syntax like (department=IT).

New-ADUser -Name "Maria Garcia" -SamAccountName mgarcia -GivenName Maria -Surname Garcia `
  -Path "OU=Sales,DC=corp,DC=local" -Department Sales -Title "Account Executive" `
  -AccountPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString "Welcome!2026x" -AsPlainText -Force) -Enabled $true

Set-ADUser mgarcia -Description "New hire" -ChangePasswordAtLogon $true
Disable-ADAccount tlee
Move-ADObject (Get-ADUser tlee) -TargetPath "OU=Disabled Users,DC=corp,DC=local"
Remove-ADUser tlee -Confirm:$false
  • An enabled account must have a password that meets the domain policy, supplied as a SecureString — hence ConvertTo-SecureString. (An account created with no password is created disabled.)
  • -Path is the DN of the OU where the object is created. -TargetPath is where Move-ADObject puts it. Moving changes the DN (but not the GUID or SID).
  • Add -WhatIf to rehearse and -Confirm to be prompted. -Confirm:$false suppresses the prompt — only use it when you are sure.

# All enabled Sales users and their titles
Get-ADUser -Filter "Department -eq 'Sales' -and Enabled -eq $true" -Properties Title |
  Select-Object Name, Title | Sort-Object Name

# Disable every account in the Contractors OU
Get-ADUser -Filter * -SearchBase "OU=Contractors,DC=corp,DC=local" | Disable-ADAccount

# Count users
(Get-ADUser -Filter *).Count

# Do something to each
Get-ADUser -Filter "Department -eq 'IT'" | ForEach-Object { Set-ADUser $_ -Description "IT staff" }

Safety habit: always run the Get- half of a pipeline by itself first to see exactly which objects it selects — then add the destructive cmdlet. Real admins have disabled the whole company with one wrong filter.

ad4.html:
A lockout policy has three numbers: the lockout threshold (bad attempts before locking, e.g. 5), the observation window (how long failed attempts are counted) and the lockout duration (how long it stays locked; 0 = until an admin unlocks). A domain with a threshold of 0 never locks accounts — and is wide open to password guessing.

Search-ADAccount -LockedOut                          # who is locked right now?
Get-ADUser jsmith -Properties LockedOut, LastLogonDate
Unlock-ADAccount -Identity jsmith

Unlocking is not the fix — find the source. If it re-locks in minutes, something is still sending the old password: a phone mail app, a mapped drive, a Windows service or scheduled task, a saved RDP credential, another PC with a stale session. On the PDC emulator, Event ID 4740 names the Caller Computer that caused the lockout.

ad4.h: Resetting a password the right way
ad4.html:
1. Verify identity first (callback number, manager approval, security questions). Social engineering of helpdesks is a top attack path.
  2. Reset to a temporary password and force a change at next logon:
Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity bwong -Reset -NewPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString "Temp#Pass2026!" -AsPlainText -Force)
Set-ADUser bwong -ChangePasswordAtLogon $true
  • -Reset = an admin sets the password without knowing the old one (needs the “Reset password” right). Without -Reset the cmdlet expects -OldPassword (the user changing their own).
  • The new password must meet the domain policy (length, complexity, history) or the reset fails.
  • Never send a password by email/chat in clear text. Prefer self-service password reset (SSPR) with MFA.
  • Reset ≠ unlock: a locked account stays locked after a reset until you also unlock it.

ad4.h: Classic tickets and what is usually wrong
ad4.html:
SymptomLikely cause → fix
"The trust relationship between this workstation and the primary domain failed"Computer account password out of sync (old image/snapshot restore). Test-ComputerSecureChannel -Repair -Credential or rejoin the domain.
"We can’t sign you in" / cannot contact the domainNo network, wrong DNS, DC down. Check ipconfig /all, nslookup corp.local.
Kerberos / odd auth errors on one PCClock skew over 5 min → w32tm /resync
Can log on but a drive/setting is missingGPO not applied: gpupdate /force, gpresult /r
"Your account has been disabled"Disabled (leaver? mistake?) → confirm with manager, then Enable-ADAccount
"This user account has expired"Account expiration date passed (contractor) → extend the date
"You must change your password"Password expired or flagged → user changes it (Ctrl+Alt+Del)
"The user cannot log on to this workstation""Log on to" workstation restriction on the account

whoami /groups              # my groups (token) on this PC
net user jsmith /domain     # quick account status
gpresult /r                 # which GPOs applied?
gpupdate /force             # refresh Group Policy now
klist                       # my Kerberos tickets
klist purge                 # throw them away (picks up new group membership)
nltest /dsgetdc:corp.local  # which DC am I using?

Group changes need a new token: adding someone to a group does not help their current session. They must log off and on (or klist purge) to get a fresh ticket with the new group. Document each ticket: what, when, what you changed, who verified — that is also your audit trail.

ad5.html:
New-ADGroup -Name "G-Finance" -GroupScope Global -Path "OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=local"
New-ADGroup -Name "DL-FinanceShare-RW" -GroupScope DomainLocal -Path "OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=local"

Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "G-Finance" -Members jdoe, rkim
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "DL-FinanceShare-RW" -Members "G-Finance"   # Global into Domain Local

Get-ADGroupMember "G-Finance"
Get-ADGroupMember "DL-FinanceShare-RW" -Recursive           # expands nested groups to users
Get-ADPrincipalGroupMembership jdoe                          # every group jdoe is in
  • -GroupScope is required: DomainLocal, Global or Universal.
  • Users do not pipe straight into Add-ADGroupMember -Members. Use -Members (Get-ADUser ...) or loop with ForEach-Object.
  • Naming conventions make groups self-documenting: G- role groups, DL- resource/permission groups, U- universal.

Accessing a file over the network passes two permission checks: the share permission and the NTFS permission. The result is the most restrictive of the two. Within NTFS, permissions from all your groups add up, but an explicit Deny beats Allow.

  • Inheritance: folders pass permissions to children unless blocked.
  • Common practice: set the share to “Authenticated Users: Change/Full” and do all real control with NTFS ACLs on groups.
  • Standard NTFS levels: Read, Read & Execute, Modify, Full Control. Never give Full Control or Everyone-write widely.
  • Use icacls or the Security tab; check Effective Access to see what a specific user would really get.

The Delegation of Control Wizard (right-click an OU in ADUC) writes ACL entries so a group can do specific jobs on that OU — typically reset passwords, unlock accounts, create/delete users, manage group membership. The helpdesk gets only what it needs, only where it needs it.

  • Delegate to a group (G-Helpdesk), never to individuals.
  • Delegation at the OU level is why OU design matters.
  • Members of protected groups (Domain Admins etc.) get their ACLs reset hourly by AdminSDHolder/SDProp, so helpdesk delegation will not work on admin accounts — by design.

• Token bloat: too many (nested) groups can overflow the Kerberos token (about 1,000+ groups) and break logon.
  • Circular nesting and deep nesting make audits painful. Keep it to AGDLP — two levels.
  • Stale membership: review quarterly. Access creep from movers is the most common audit finding.
  • Direct user ACLs: permissions assigned to individuals instead of groups become unmanageable.
  • Group changes apply at the user’s next logon.

ad6.html:
A Group Policy Object is a bundle of settings pushed to computers and users. It has two halves: the Group Policy Container (GPC) in AD (metadata) and the Group Policy Template (GPT) in SYSVOL (the actual files). Each GPO has a Computer Configuration (applies at boot to the machine, regardless of who logs on) and a User Configuration (applies at sign-in to that user, wherever they log on).

  • Two default GPOs: Default Domain Policy (linked to the domain; holds the domain-wide password, lockout and Kerberos policy) and Default Domain Controllers Policy. Best practice: change only the account policy in the first one; create new GPOs for everything else.
  • Typical settings: password/lockout rules, mapped drives and printers (Group Policy Preferences), screen-lock timeout, Windows Update/WSUS, firewall rules, AppLocker, block USB storage, audit policy, PowerShell logging, LAPS.

Policies apply in this order and the last one applied wins on a conflict:

Local → Site → Domain → OU (parent OU first, then child OUs)

  • Inheritance: child OUs inherit the GPOs linked above them.
  • Link order: several GPOs on one container — the one with the lowest link-order number has the highest precedence (it is applied last).
  • Block Inheritance (set on an OU) stops parent GPOs from flowing down.
  • Enforced (set on a GPO link; formerly “No Override”) forces the GPO to apply even through Block Inheritance and wins conflicts against lower-level GPOs. Enforced beats Block.
  • Security filtering: a GPO applies only to principals with Read + Apply group policy on it (default: Authenticated Users). WMI filters add conditions (e.g. only Windows 11). Loopback processing applies the computer’s user settings no matter who signs in (kiosks, labs).

• Workstations/servers refresh every 90 minutes + a random 0–30 minute offset; domain controllers every 5 minutes. Also at boot (computer) and sign-in (user).
  • gpupdate /force re-applies now. Some settings need a reboot or logoff.
  • gpresult /r — which GPOs applied or were filtered out, and why. gpresult /h report.html — full HTML report. Run it on the affected PC, as the affected user.
  • Group Policy Modeling predicts, Results reports what really happened.
  • Check: is the object in the right OU? Is the link enabled? Security filtering/WMI? Replication of SYSVOL? DNS? Time?
  • Test first: link new GPOs to a test OU before production. A bad GPO linked to the domain can lock out every user.
  • Never store passwords in Group Policy Preferences (the old “cpassword” is trivially decryptable — MS14-025).

Get-GPO -All
New-GPO -Name "Workstation Lockdown"
New-GPLink -Name "Workstation Lockdown" -Target "OU=Workstations,DC=corp,DC=local"
Set-GPLink -Name "Security Baseline" -Target "DC=corp,DC=local" -Enforced Yes
Set-GPInheritance -Target "OU=Servers,DC=corp,DC=local" -IsBlocked Yes
Get-GPInheritance -Target "OU=Servers,DC=corp,DC=local"   # what really reaches this OU?
Backup-GPO -Name "Workstation Lockdown" -Path C:\GPOBackup

Get-GPInheritance is your “what applies here?” answer. -Target is always the DN of the site, domain or OU.

Fine-Grained Password Policies (Password Settings Objects, created in the Active Directory Administrative Center or New-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy) let different groups — e.g. admins — have stricter password rules than the domain default; they attach to users/groups, not OUs.

ad7.html:
Kerberos proves identity with tickets issued by the Key Distribution Center (KDC) that runs on every DC. Your password never crosses the network.

  1. AS-REQ — you ask the KDC for a Ticket Granting Ticket, proving you know your password by encrypting a timestamp with your key (pre-authentication).
  2. AS-REP — the KDC returns a TGT, encrypted with the krbtgt account’s key (only the KDC can read it).
  3. TGS-REQ — to reach a service (cifs/fs01.corp.local), you present the TGT and ask for a service ticket.
  4. TGS-REP — the KDC returns a service ticket encrypted with the service account’s key, containing your group SIDs (the PAC).
  5. AP-REQ — you give the ticket to the file server.
  6. AP-REP — (optional) the server proves itself to you: mutual authentication.
  • Port 88. Tickets default to 10 hours (renewable 7 days). Clock skew limit: 5 minutes.
  • Services are identified by SPNs (Service Principal Names), e.g. MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local:1433. Using a server’s IP address instead of its name breaks Kerberos and falls back to NTLM.
  • klist shows your tickets; klist purge clears them.

NTLM is the older challenge–response protocol: the server sends a challenge, the client answers with a response derived from the NT hash of the password. Used when Kerberos is unavailable (IP address, workgroup, no DC reachable). Weaknesses: the hash itself is the credential (pass-the-hash), responses can be relayed, and offline cracking is fast. Hardening: require SMB signing, disable LLMNR/NBT-NS, restrict or audit NTLM, put admins in Protected Users, and prefer Kerberos.

IDMeaning
4624Successful logon. Logon Type: 2 interactive, 3 network, 4 batch, 5 service, 7 unlock, 10 RDP (RemoteInteractive), 11 cached
4625Failed logon (Status/SubStatus: 0xC000006A bad password, 0xC0000064 no such user, 0xC0000234 locked out, 0xC0000072 disabled)
4634 / 4647Logoff
4648Logon with explicit credentials (runas, lateral movement)
4672Special privileges assigned to a new logon (an admin signed in)
4720 / 4722 / 4725 / 4726User created / enabled / disabled / deleted
4723 / 4724Password change (user) / reset (admin)
4728 / 4732 / 4756Member added to a Global / Local / Universal security group
4740 / 4767Account locked out / unlocked
4768Kerberos TGT requested
4769Kerberos service ticket requested
4771Kerberos pre-authentication failed
4776NTLM credential validation by a DC
1102The Security log was cleared — an attacker hiding tracks

• Brute force: many 4625s against one account, then maybe a 4740 lockout.
  • Password spray: a few attempts each across many accounts from one source, staying under the lockout threshold — many 4625/4771 with different usernames, same IP.
  • Success after failures: a 4625 burst followed by a 4624 for the same account = the guess worked.
  • Privilege creep / persistence: 4720 (new account) then 4728/4732 (added to Domain Admins) within minutes.
  • Lateral movement: 4624 type 3 (network) and type 10 (RDP) from unusual workstations, 4648 with explicit credentials.
  • Kerberoasting: a burst of 4769 events from one account asking for many service tickets, often with ticket encryption type 0x17 (RC4).
  • AS-REP roasting: 4768 requests with pre-authentication type 0 (none).
  • Log tampering: 1102.

ad8.html:
AD is multi-master (any DC accepts changes), but a few jobs must be done by exactly one DC — Flexible Single Master Operations roles:

RoleScopeJob
Schema MasterForestOnly DC allowed to change the schema
Domain Naming MasterForestAdds/removes domains and application partitions
PDC EmulatorDomainAuthoritative time source, handles password changes/lockouts urgently, preferred GPO editing target, legacy NT compatibility. The busiest role.
RID MasterDomainHands out pools of RIDs so every DC can create unique SIDs
Infrastructure MasterDomainUpdates cross-domain object references
netdom query fsmo
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object PDCEmulator, RIDMaster, InfrastructureMaster
  • Transfer = planned, graceful (old DC alive). Seize = emergency when the holder is dead for good; the old DC must never be brought back online.

ad8.h: Replication, sites and the Global Catalog
ad8.html:
• Sites map IP subnets to physical locations. Replication inside a site is fast (changes notify within about 15 seconds; password changes and lockouts replicate urgently). Between sites it follows a schedule (default every 180 minutes, minimum 15) over site links. Clients also use sites to pick the closest DC.
  • The KCC (Knowledge Consistency Checker) builds the replication topology automatically. Conflicts resolve by version number, timestamp, GUID (last writer wins).
  • Check health: repadmin /replsummary, repadmin /showrepl, dcdiag /v.
  • Global Catalog (GC): a DC that also holds a read-only partial copy of every object in the forest. Needed for UPN logons, searching the whole forest and expanding Universal group membership at logon. Every site should have a GC (ports 3268/3269).
  • RODC (Read-Only DC) for branch offices: holds no password hashes by default (a Password Replication Policy chooses what is cached), so a stolen RODC is a smaller disaster.
  • SYSVOL replicates with DFSR, separately from AD replication.

• Back up System State on at least two DCs regularly (it includes NTDS.dit, SYSVOL, registry). Test restores.
  • AD Recycle Bin (must be enabled once per forest; cannot be turned off) keeps deleted objects with all attributes and group memberships for the deleted object lifetime (default 180 days), then they sit as recycled objects until the tombstone lifetime ends. Without it, a deleted user comes back as an empty shell (tombstone) and loses memberships.
# Find, then restore ONLY what you mean to
Get-ADObject -Filter "samAccountName -eq 'pnair'" -IncludeDeletedObjects
Get-ADObject -Filter "samAccountName -eq 'pnair'" -IncludeDeletedObjects | Restore-ADObject
  • Authoritative restore (in DSRM with ntdsutil) forces a restored older version to overwrite newer replicas; non-authoritative restore gets overwritten by replication.
  • Never roll back a DC with a plain VM snapshot — USN rollback corrupts replication. Use VM-GenerationID–aware platforms and AD-aware backups.
  • Prevent disaster: Protect from accidental deletion on OUs, restricted delete rights, change alerts.

TrustNotes
Parent–child, Tree-rootAutomatic, two-way, transitive inside a forest
ShortcutManual, speeds authentication between two domains in a big forest
ForestManual, transitive between two forest roots
ExternalManual, non-transitive, to a single domain outside the forest
RealmTo a non-Windows Kerberos realm

Direction: if A trusts B, then B’s users can be given access to A’s resources (the arrow of trust points opposite to access). SID filtering blocks SID-history abuse across trusts. Always use AD-integrated DNS zones with secure dynamic updates, and point DCs at themselves/each other for DNS — not at ISP resolvers.

ad9.h: Why AD is the crown jewel
ad9.html:
If an attacker controls AD, they control every domain-joined system and every identity. Most ransomware incidents end with domain admin. A typical intrusion chain (conceptual, for defenders):

  1. Recon: enumerate users, groups, trusts and attack paths (tools like BloodHound map “who can become Domain Admin”).
  2. Initial access: phishing, exposed RDP/VPN, password spraying.
  3. Privilege escalation: Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, weak ACLs/delegation, passwords in scripts or GPP, vulnerable certificate templates (AD CS).
  4. Credential theft: dumping LSASS memory, pass-the-hash, pass-the-ticket.
  5. Lateral movement: SMB/RDP/WinRM/PsExec using stolen credentials.
  6. Domain dominance: DCSync (abusing replication rights to pull every hash), copying NTDS.dit, Golden Ticket (forged TGT using the krbtgt hash).
  7. Persistence: hidden admin accounts, AdminSDHolder ACL changes, SID history, rogue GPOs.

Kerberoasting: any authenticated domain user can ask the KDC for a service ticket for any account that has an SPN. That ticket is encrypted with the service account’s password hash, so the attacker takes it offline and cracks it with no lockouts and no alerts. Service accounts often have weak, never-expiring passwords and excess privilege.

  • Defend: use gMSA (group Managed Service Accounts — 120-character auto-rotated passwords) where possible; otherwise 25+ character random passwords; least privilege; disable RC4 so tickets use AES; monitor bursts of 4769.
  • Hunt: Get-ADUser -Filter "ServicePrincipalName -like '*'" -Properties ServicePrincipalName

AS-REP roasting: an account flagged “Do not require Kerberos preauthentication” lets anyone request an encrypted blob for it without knowing the password — also crackable offline. Defend: never set that flag; find and fix: Get-ADUser -Filter "DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true" and Set-ADAccountControl <user> -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $false.

• Least privilege: Domain Admins should contain only a handful of dedicated admin accounts — never a person’s everyday account. Keep Enterprise/Schema Admins empty. Review privileged groups monthly.
  • Separate admin accounts (jsmith vs jsmith-adm) and Privileged Access Workstations.
  • Tiered model: Tier 0 = DCs, AD, identity systems; Tier 1 = servers/apps; Tier 2 = workstations/users. An account from a higher tier must never log on to a lower tier (stolen credentials on a laptop must not reach a DC).
  • LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) gives every PC a unique, rotating local admin password so one stolen hash does not unlock them all.
  • Protected Users group; Credential Guard (protects secrets in LSASS); disable LLMNR/NBT-NS and legacy NTLM/SMBv1; require SMB and LDAP signing.
  • Account hygiene: disable or delete stale accounts (no sign-in for 90+ days), reduce PasswordNeverExpires exceptions, remove unused SPNs, ban weak/breached passwords, enforce MFA.
  • krbtgt: after a suspected compromise, reset its password twice (12+ hours apart) to invalidate Golden Tickets.
  • AdminSDHolder: protects accounts with adminCount=1; attackers modify it for persistence — audit it.

ad9.h: Detect, respond, and audit with PowerShell
ad9.html:
Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 90.00:00:00 -UsersOnly   # stale accounts
Get-ADGroupMember "Domain Admins" -Recursive                          # who is really admin?
Get-ADUser -Filter "PasswordNeverExpires -eq $true" -Properties PasswordNeverExpires
Get-ADUser -Filter "ServicePrincipalName -like '*'" -Properties ServicePrincipalName
Get-ADUser -Filter "DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true"
  • Alert on: membership changes to privileged groups (4728/4732/4756), new accounts (4720), log cleared (1102), DCSync-style replication from non-DCs (4662 with the replication GUIDs), spikes in 4769/4625/4771.
  • Incident steps: contain (isolate hosts, disable suspect accounts), identify scope, rotate credentials (privileged accounts, service accounts, krbtgt twice), review GPOs/ACLs/AdminSDHolder/scheduled tasks for backdoors, rebuild compromised DCs from known-good media, then monitor.
  • Use Microsoft Defender for Identity (or equivalent) for behavioral detection.
